query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: HEA nanoparticles with identical equiatomic compositions will exhibit significantly delayed premelting onset and higher melting temperatures when post-synthesis annealed to induce chemical short-range order (SRO), compared to nanoparticles that are rapidly quenched to retain a random atomic distribution.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HEA nanoparticles (e.g., CoFeNiCr or CoFeNiMn) synthesized via a kinetic route (e.g., laser ablation) with a narrow size distribution (<10 nm) and near-equimolar elemental composition.
generation.intervention: Post-synthesis thermal annealing at a controlled temperature (e.g., 800–900 K) for a fixed duration to promote SRO formation, versus rapid quenching to room temperature to suppress SRO.
generation.conditions: Nanoparticles should be embedded within an inert matrix or supported on a substrate to minimize flux effects, and heated in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., argon) using in situ high-resolution TEM or differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) in the temperature region spanning 800 K to 975 K.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of local atomic order (SRO) within the nanoparticle core, as detected by changes in pair-correlation functions or selected area diffraction patterns, which lowers the Gibbs free energy.
generation.mechanism: Chemical SRO enhances local bonding interactions and increases effective mixing entropy stabilization, thereby retarding surface disorder and amorphization that typically drive premelting. In contrast, random solid solutions lack this additional stabilization, leading to earlier onset of surface-driven premelting phenomena.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed (SRO-enhanced) nanoparticles will exhibit a higher melting point (by an approximate range of tens to over a hundred Kelvin) and a delayed premelting behavior (observable via structural changes) compared to the rapidly quenched nanoparticles. Relative to the baseline (randomly quenched nanoparticles), the SRO-enhanced particles will show reduced surface diffusivity and a higher fraction of crystalline core at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized by laser ablation and quenched immediately to room temperature, thereby retaining a largely random solid-solution structure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for equiatomic HEA nanoparticles in the nanoscale regime (typically <10 nm) and within an operational temperature range of approximately 800 K to 975 K. Deviation outside this range or for significantly different particle sizes may involve additional mechanisms such as size-dependent surface melting.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the melting point shift and the quantitative degree of SRO may vary with nanoparticle size, composition fluctuations, and annealing time/temperature. There is also uncertainty regarding the sensitivity of in situ techniques to detect low levels of SRO in such small particles.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with identical size distributions via laser ablation. Subject one batch to controlled annealing intended to induce SRO, while quenching the other batch immediately to preserve a random structure. Use in situ high-resolution TEM heating experiments and DSC to monitor the onset of premelting and measure the melting temperature of each batch.
measurements: Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns to detect changes in chemical ordering.
DSC thermograms to determine melting onset and melting point.
High-resolution TEM images to observe surface disorder and amorphization patterns during heating.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally annealed nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant increase in melting temperature/delayed premelting onset compared to the quenched nanoparticles, or if no differences in SRO indicators are observed between the two groups, then the hypothesis that SRO governs premelting/melting behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To date, recognizing the SRO structure of HEAs in experiments has been fairly challenging. Mössbauer spectroscopy is a good tool to exactly probe SRO, but it is usually limited in binary alloys containing Fe. It is because the neighbouring atom (the species different from Fe) around the 57Fe nuclei probe is assumed to be measurable by analysing the variation of spectral hyperfine parameters. However, with increasing constituent elements, the spectral hyperfine parameters become much more sophisticated so that it hardly distinguishes the individual element effect around the 57Fe nuclei probe. Another experimental method, transmission electron microscopy, observed the SRO in VCoNi. Unfortunately, the evidence of SRO from experiments is missing for HEAs composed of more constituent elements. Nevertheless, the study on Fe–Cr binary alloys revealed the SRO phenomenon in the Fe–Cr samples. This may also be related to the low electronegativity and the resulting negative stress of Cr, similar to our study. We expect more novel experimental methods to unleash feasible and explicit evidence of the SRO phenomenon in multi-principal element alloys.

From Fig. 6(a), it is evident that equiatomic CoFeNiCr and CoFeNiMn HEAs exhibit correlations positioned at the lower end, implying that this equiatomic elemental composition promotes the thermal stability of the alloy system, thus validating the requirement of equiatomic or nearly equiatomic composition in the definition of HEAs. The thermal stability of the Cr-rich Cr54 HEA is comparatively worse, and according to the correlations between the change in Gibbs free energy and temperature, a phase transition in this alloy system occurs at T = 883 K. Comparing the SQS and SRO structures of the CoFeNiCr HEA, it is observed that the thermal stability of the structure after MC iterations is better than that of the initial random structure. This suggests that chemical ordering contributes to the enhancement of the thermal stability of HEAs. In the case of the CoFeNiMn HEA, lacking chemical ordering, the correlations between the change in Gibbs free energy and temperature in the structures before and after MC iterations are relatively close. AbstractUsing the molecular dynamics method, the melting character, mechanical properties, microstructures, and strain deformation mechanisms of nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy are systematically investigated in the present work. The simulation results suggest that the melting point in CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy decreases with the grain size, decreasing from 3.6 to 2.0 nm. The grain size has a significant effect on shear and Young’s modulus compared to bulk modulus. The stress-strain simulation demonstrates that the ultimate tensile strength decreases with the decrease of the grain size, while the plastic deformation increases with the decrease in grain size. While the average grain size decreases to 2.0 nm, the amorphization induced by small grain size reduces plastic deformation. The common neighbor analysis shows that the face-centered cubic (FCC) composition of CoCrFeNiMn decreases gradually with decreasing grain size. For the sample with a grain size of 2.0 nm, the FCC composition is about 19% at a strain of 20%, accompanied by severe amorphization. papers.title: Unveiling the mechanism of tuning elemental distribution in high entropy alloys and its effect on thermal stability.
papers.system: Equiatomic high‐entropy alloys (e.g., CoFeNiCr and CoFeNiMn) including a Cr‐rich variant
papers.approach: DFT calculations combined with Monte Carlo simulations comparing random solid-solutions (SQS) versus chemically ordered (SRO) structures; analysis of Gibbs free energy changes with temperature.
papers.findings: Equiatomic HEAs with near-equal composition and detectable SRO exhibit enhanced thermal stability relative to Cr-rich systems. The studies report that after MC iterations the ordered (SRO) configuration exhibits lower Gibbs free energy and higher stability at temperatures around 800–975 K, while alloys lacking chemical ordering show less marked stabilization.
papers.mechanism: Chemical short-range order reduces the free energy by locally optimizing bonding interactions, thereby retarding disorder-induced phase transitions and premelting phenomena.

papers.title: Melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides by deep learning potentials.
papers.approach: Atomistic melting simulations in a constant-pressure (NPT) ensemble using deep neural network (machine learning) interatomic potentials with stepwise heating and cooling protocols.
papers.findings: The simulations show that increasing the nitrogen content leads to an increase in the calculated melting temperature, with a nonlinear enhancement observed (maximum melting temperature around 3580 ± 30 K for (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25). Detailed analysis of pair correlations and entropy calculations in the liquid phase supports this result.
papers.mechanism: The nitrogen addition modifies local bonding and increases the effective mixing entropy in the system, thus stabilizing the solid phase against premelting; the non‐linear behavior is explained by changes in pair correlations and entropy contributions.

papers.title: Atomic Simulations of Grain Structures and Deformation Behaviors in Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations varying average grain sizes (from ~3.6 nm down to ~2.0 nm) to assess melting behavior, mechanical properties, and amorphization tendencies.
papers.findings: The simulations indicate that the melting temperature decreases with a decrease in grain size (e.g., ~1430 K for 3.6 nm grains and further reduced for smaller grains). Smaller grains lead to enhanced surface effects and premature amorphization, with a marked reduction in the FCC phase fraction at high temperature.
papers.mechanism: In small nanoparticles, a higher surface-to-volume ratio and the presence of low-coordination sites promote premelting due to surface disorder and amorphization, which decrease overall thermal stability compared to bulk or larger-grained counterparts.

papers.title: Kinetically-controlled laser-synthesis of colloidal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
papers.approach: Ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation in liquid to synthesize nanoparticles followed by structural characterization using XRD, SAED, and HRTEM; analysis of size, composition uniformity, and surface segregation effects.
papers.findings: The nanoparticles, with diameters below 5 nm, retain an equimolar composition and a crystalline fcc lattice. For larger nanoparticles, evidence of defect structures and surface segregation (particularly of more oxidation-prone elements) suggests kinetic control during synthesis influences the final phase and possibly affects the melting behavior.
papers.mechanism: The kinetic constraints during rapid laser ablation lead to a metastable, near-equimolar crystalline state. Surface segregation and defect formations induced by different cooling rates may govern local melting and premelting phenomena by altering the stability of the particle surfaces.

established: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions with chemical SRO display enhanced thermal stability.
Melting temperatures of high-entropy systems are sensitive to composition adjustments (e.g., nitrogen content) and particle size.
Computational melting curves correlate changes in Gibbs free energy (including entropy contributions) with thermal stability.
Kinetic synthesis methods like laser ablation can yield metastable HEA nanoparticles with unique melting and premelting characteristics.

approaches_tried.approach: DFT and Monte Carlo simulations comparing random (SQS) versus chemically ordered (SRO) structures.
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that chemical ordering lowers the Gibbs free energy and improves thermal stability in HEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Deep learning potential-based atomistic melting simulations under controlled heating/cooling in the NPT ensemble.
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified a nonlinear increase in melting temperature with nitrogen content and provided insight into the role of local bonding and entropy.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations of nanoparticle systems with varying grain sizes.
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that reduced grain sizes lead to premelting via enhanced surface effects and amorphization.

approaches_tried.approach: Ultrafast laser synthesis to produce colloidal HEA nanoparticles and subsequent structural characterization.
approaches_tried.outcome: Showed that rapid quenching and kinetic control produce metastable nanoparticles with potential for unique premelting behavior due to surface defects and segregation.

mechanisms: Enhanced thermal stability via chemical short-range ordering (SRO) that lowers the system’s free energy.
Influence of nanoparticle size and resulting surface-to-volume ratio on premelting through surface disorder and amorphization.
Modification of local bonding and entropy contributions through compositional adjustments (e.g., nitrogen incorporation) that tune melting behavior.
Kinetic effects during rapid synthesis (e.g., laser ablation) leading to metastable structures with surface segregation that may alter melting characteristics.
disagreements: The relative contributions of chemical ordering (SRO) versus surface-induced disorder (grain size effects) in governing the melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles remain debated.

While some studies emphasize the role of entropy and mixing (via compositional adjustments) in stabilizing the lattice, others highlight that kinetic synthesis routes can introduce defects and segregation that modify melting characteristics.
open_questions: How do surface effects and intrinsic chemical ordering interplay to control premelting and melting behaviors in HEA nanoparticles?
What is the critical size or compositional window over which the proposed mechanisms (SRO vs. surface disorder) dominate the melting behavior?
Can a controlled comparison between equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with induced SRO and those with intentionally suppressed ordering definitively reveal the governing factor?
How do rapid synthesis kinetics (e.g., in laser ablation) affect the balance between bulk-like entropy stabilization and surface defect formation in determining thermal stability?
opportunities: Perform controlled experiments comparing nanoparticles synthesized with identical compositions but differing thermal histories to vary the degree of SRO versus surface disorder.
Design in situ heating experiments (e.g., using TEM or synchrotron XRD) on size-selected HEA nanoparticles to directly correlate grain size and chemical ordering with melting onset.

Combine deep learning-based simulations with advanced synthesis methods to predict and validate the impact of compositional tweaks (such as varying nitrogen or other interstitials) on melting temperatures.

Investigate the influence of kinetic synthesis parameters (e.g., laser pulse energy, cooling rates) on the formation of surface segregation, correlating these with subsequent melting behavior under thermal stress.

directions.direction: Composition and annealing treatment to control chemical short-range order (SRO) versus random atomic distributions in HEA nanoparticles.
directions.assessment: This approach directly tests whether the presence of chemical SRO is the controlling factor for premelting/melting behavior. Prior evidence (e.g., record IDs PMC11265590::web::022 and PMC11265590::web::019) shows that SRO lowers the Gibbs free energy and improves thermal stability, and controlled annealing is a feasible way to induce or suppress SRO while keeping composition and size constant.

directions.direction: Synthesis route variation through laser ablation conditions to modulate kinetic trapping, surface defect density, and segregation versus equilibrium chemical ordering.
directions.assessment: By varying the synthesis parameters (for instance, laser pulse energy or cooling rate), one may generate nanoparticles that are either kinetically trapped with significant surface segregation or closer to equilibrium with enhanced internal ordering. This route can explore the interplay between surface effects and bulk ordering but may conflate surface segregation with SRO effects, making interpretation more challenging.

directions.direction: Surface engineering via passivation coatings that selectively inhibit surface-induced premelting while leaving the nanoparticle core intact.
directions.assessment: This method isolates surface contributions by comparing coated and uncoated nanoparticles. However, although it shows the role of surface disorder, it does not directly test the hypothesis regarding the mechanism of bulk chemical ordering (SRO) as the governing factor for melting behavior.

directions.direction: In situ experimental characterization using high-resolution TEM with heating stages to directly observe the onset of premelting associated with differing degrees of SRO versus amorphous surface disorder.
directions.assessment: This approach provides a real-time view of microstructural changes during heating and can correlate the atomic-scale ordering (via diffraction contrast or real-space imaging) with premelting behavior. It is highly informative but requires precursors with well-characterized prior SRO states, which likely must be prepared using controlled annealing.

directions.direction: Atomistic simulations (MD or Monte Carlo) with deep learning potentials to model HEA nanoparticles having SRO and random structures.
directions.assessment: Simulations allow one to individually alter SRO and surface disorder variables to predict melting curves at the atomic level. This approach is well supported by previous simulation work (e.g., PMC11576752::web::013) but benefits most if validated by experiments. The challenge is ensuring that the predicted behavior can be distinctly attributed to SRO while matching experimental nanoparticle conditions.

choice.direction: Composition and annealing treatment to control chemical SRO in HEA nanoparticles.
choice.why: This direction directly targets the core open question—whether the intrinsic atomic ordering (SRO) governs the premelting and melting behavior. By using controlled thermal annealing to induce SRO in otherwise identically synthesized nanoparticles, one can directly compare the melting behavior with that of nanoparticles that remain in a random solid solution. Prior evidence supports the role of SRO in stabilizing HEAs at elevated temperatures (see PMC11265590::web::022 and PMC11265590::web::019), and the approach complies with application-related constraints while being experimentally feasible.
